First woman in space — Valentina Tereshkova, 48 orbits

Vostok 6 carried Valentina Tereshkova, and made her the first woman in space — a fact that stood alone for nineteen years and went unmatched by the United States until 1983. She was not a pilot but a textile worker and amateur parachutist, chosen in part for exactly that symbolism: proof, the Soviet program said, that in the workers' state even the frontier of space was open to anyone. Whatever the motive, forty-eight orbits later the milestone was real and permanent, and it would be two decades before any other nation could say it had done the same.

Valentina Tereshkova's 48-orbit, 2-day-23-hour flight — the first woman in space, and still the only woman ever to have flown a solo space mission. Selected from a group of five female cosmonaut candidates assembled in 1962, Tereshkova launched 1963-06-16 09:30 UTC, only 2 years after Gagarin's first orbital flight. Her capsule programmed for an upward-rather-than-downward orbit-correction burn — she manually identified the error and ground controllers supplied corrective data. Landed 1963-06-19 08:20 UTC near Bayevo, Altai Krai. Tereshkova later became a senior figure in Soviet politics and remains the youngest woman ever flown to orbit at 26 years.
Pre-loaded attitude software would have raised orbit instead of lowering it; ground controllers supplied corrective data.
Landed near Bayevo, Altai Krai, 1963-06-19 08:20 UTC after 48 orbits.
